lec05kp01-u01-p1-title.name: u01-p1-title
lec05kp01-u01-p1-title.text: Same four points, new labels: one line seems enough for OR and AND, but XOR puts classes diagonally

lec05kp01-u01-p1-bridge.name: u01-p1-bridge
lec05kp01-u01-p1-bridge.text: Chapter 3 let a model decide the class with one line. If only the labels of the same four points change, can that model still answer?

lec05kp01-u01-p1-nf-lec05-kp01-p1-1.name: fig:lec05-kp01-p1|Three panels of the same four points labelled OR (0111), AND (0001) and XOR (0110); A circles, B squares.

lec05kp01-u01-p1-nf-lec05-kp01-p1-55.name: term:Label
lec05kp01-u01-p1-nf-lec05-kp01-p1-55.text:
Label: the class a point must go to:
A (circle, output 1) or B (square, output 0).

lec05kp01-u01-p1-nf-lec05-kp01-p1-56.name: term:Exclusive OR
lec05kp01-u01-p1-nf-lec05-kp01-p1-56.text:
Exclusive OR (XOR): outputs 1 only if the two
inputs differ, otherwise 0.

lec05kp01-u01-p1-nf-lec05-kp01-p1-58.name: fig:lec05-kp01-p1#58
lec05kp01-u01-p1-nf-lec05-kp01-p1-58.text:
The four points are identical; only the labels differ.
Outputs in the order (0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1):
OR is 0111, AND is 0001, XOR is 0110.
(computed)

lec05kp01-u01-p2-title.name: u01-p2-title
lec05kp01-u01-p2-title.text: Positive score means A: OR with g = x₁ + x₂ − 0.5 puts all three A points on the positive side

lec05kp01-u01-p2-bridge.name: u01-p2-bridge
lec05kp01-u01-p2-bridge.text: The A points of OR take three corners, AND only one, and XOR puts same-class points on the diagonals. How does one line give scores and decide the class?

lec05kp01-u01-p2-nf-lec05-kp01-p2-1.name: fig:lec05-kp01-p2|OR line x1 + x2 = 0.5 with the positive side shaded; scores -0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 1.5; the three A points are on the positive side.

lec05kp01-u01-p2-nf-lec05-kp01-p2-4.name: fig:lec05-kp01-p2#4
lec05kp01-u01-p2-nf-lec05-kp01-p2-4.text: Give every point a score: positive means class A

lec05kp01-u01-p2-nf-lec05-kp01-p2-10.name: term:Score
lec05kp01-u01-p2-nf-lec05-kp01-p2-10.text:
Score: the number you get by putting a point into g;
its sign says which side of the line it is on. Exactly 0
is also B, and the rule may not change after seeing
the labels.

lec05kp01-u01-p2-nf-lec05-kp01-p2-11.name: term:Linearly separable
lec05kp01-u01-p2-nf-lec05-kp01-p2-11.text:
Linearly separable: there exists a set of coefficients
w₁, w₂, w₀ that classifies every point correctly by this
rule. The point is existence, not just the set found.

lec05kp01-u01-p2-nf-lec05-kp01-p2-13.name: fig:lec05-kp01-p2#13
lec05kp01-u01-p2-nf-lec05-kp01-p2-13.text: Example: OR with g = x₁ + x₂ − 0.5

lec05kp01-u01-p2-nf-lec05-kp01-p2-33.name: fig:lec05-kp01-p2#33
lec05kp01-u01-p2-nf-lec05-kp01-p2-33.text: yellow line: x₁ + x₂ = 0.5; blue is the positive side

lec05kp01-u01-p2-nf-lec05-kp01-p2-34.name: fig:lec05-kp01-p2#34
lec05kp01-u01-p2-nf-lec05-kp01-p2-34.text:
The four scores are −0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 1.5; the last three are
positive and called A: exactly OR. (computed)

lec05kp01-u01-p3-title.name: u01-p3-title
lec05kp01-u01-p3-title.text: The same line gets OR right but XOR wrong at 1 point: accuracy 3/4 = 75%

lec05kp01-u01-p3-bridge.name: u01-p3-bridge
lec05kp01-u01-p3-bridge.text: The OR scores are −0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 1.5 and all three A points are on the positive side. What happens when the same line is applied to XOR?

lec05kp01-u01-p3-nf-lec05-kp01-p3-1.name: fig:lec05-kp01-p3|Table for g = x1 + x2 - 0.5 on XOR: scores -0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 1.5; predictions B, A, A, A; (1,1) is wrong; accuracy 3/4 = 75%.

lec05kp01-u01-p3-nf-lec05-kp01-p3-4.name: fig:lec05-kp01-p3#4
lec05kp01-u01-p3-nf-lec05-kp01-p3-4.text: The same line g = x₁ + x₂ − 0.5 applied to XOR

lec05kp01-u01-p3-nf-lec05-kp01-p3-34.name: fig:lec05-kp01-p3#34
lec05kp01-u01-p3-nf-lec05-kp01-p3-34.text: The predictions equal OR; on XOR one point is wrong.

lec05kp01-u01-p3-nf-lec05-kp01-p3-38.name: fig:lec05-kp01-p3#38
lec05kp01-u01-p3-nf-lec05-kp01-p3-38.text: The four points and the line

lec05kp01-u01-p3-nf-lec05-kp01-p3-54.name: fig:lec05-kp01-p3#54
lec05kp01-u01-p3-nf-lec05-kp01-p3-54.text:
(1, 1) is B
yet on the
A side

lec05kp01-u01-p3-nf-lec05-kp01-p3-55.name: fig:lec05-kp01-p3#55
lec05kp01-u01-p3-nf-lec05-kp01-p3-55.text:
That is the result for this one line only; it does not yet
show that every line fails.

lec05kp01-u01-p4-title.name: u01-p4-title
lec05kp01-u01-p4-title.text: Three other lines make 2, 3 and 1 errors, but trying three lines is not a proof

lec05kp01-u01-p4-bridge.name: u01-p4-bridge
lec05kp01-u01-p4-bridge.text: The same line gets XOR wrong at 1 point, 75% accuracy. Would another line do better?

lec05kp01-u01-p4-nf-lec05-kp01-p4-1.name: fig:lec05-kp01-p4|Three lines on XOR: x1 - 0.5 predicts (0,0,1,1) with 2 errors; x1 + x2 - 1.5 predicts (0,0,0,1) with 3 errors; x1 - x2 predicts (0,0,1,0) with 1 error.

lec05kp01-u01-p4-nf-lec05-kp01-p4-64.name: fig:lec05-kp01-p4#64
lec05kp01-u01-p4-nf-lec05-kp01-p4-64.text:
All three have errors, but this is no proof: too many lines are untried.
Order (0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1); two points on the third line score 0 and are called B. (computed)

lec05kp01-u01-p5-title.name: u01-p5-title
lec05kp01-u01-p5-title.text: The two A scores add up to a positive number, and so does the score at the midpoint M

lec05kp01-u01-p5-bridge.name: u01-p5-bridge
lec05kp01-u01-p5-bridge.text: All three lines tried have errors, but too many lines are untried. How can we rule out every line at once?

lec05kp01-u01-p5-nf-lec05-kp01-p5-1.name: fig:lec05-kp01-p5|Diagonal between the two A points (0,1) and (1,0) with midpoint M = (1/2, 1/2); g(0,1) > 0, g(1,0) > 0 so w1 + w2 + 2w0 > 0 and g(M) > 0.

lec05kp01-u01-p5-nf-lec05-kp01-p5-4.name: fig:lec05-kp01-p5#4
lec05kp01-u01-p5-nf-lec05-kp01-p5-4.text: The two A points form a diagonal with midpoint M

lec05kp01-u01-p5-nf-lec05-kp01-p5-21.name: fig:lec05-kp01-p5#21
lec05kp01-u01-p5-nf-lec05-kp01-p5-21.text: Suppose some coefficients classify XOR perfectly

lec05kp01-u01-p5-nf-lec05-kp01-p5-24.name: fig:lec05-kp01-p5#24
lec05kp01-u01-p5-nf-lec05-kp01-p5-24.text: A positive plus a positive stays positive; add the two:

lec05kp01-u01-p5-nf-lec05-kp01-p5-27.name: term:Midpoint
lec05kp01-u01-p5-nf-lec05-kp01-p5-27.text:
Midpoint M: the exact middle of the segment joining the two A points,
M = (½, ½).

lec05kp01-u01-p5-nf-lec05-kp01-p5-30.name: fig:lec05-kp01-p5#30
lec05kp01-u01-p5-nf-lec05-kp01-p5-30.text:
g is linear, so g(M) is exactly the average of the two end
scores, and it is positive too.

lec05kp01-u01-p5-nf-lec05-kp01-p5-31.name: fig:lec05-kp01-p5#31
lec05kp01-u01-p5-nf-lec05-kp01-p5-31.text: Next: what condition do the two B points give?

lec05kp01-u01-p6-title.name: u01-p6-title
lec05kp01-u01-p6-title.text: The B scores add up to at most 0, contradicting A on the same expression: no line works

lec05kp01-u01-p6-bridge.name: u01-p6-bridge
lec05kp01-u01-p6-bridge.text: The two A scores add up to a positive number, and so does the score at the midpoint M. What condition do the two B points give?

lec05kp01-u01-p6-nf-lec05-kp01-p6-1.name: fig:lec05-kp01-p6|Both diagonals share the midpoint M; A needs w1 + w2 + 2w0 > 0 and B needs w1 + w2 + 2w0 <= 0, a contradiction for every line.

lec05kp01-u01-p6-nf-lec05-kp01-p6-4.name: fig:lec05-kp01-p6#4
lec05kp01-u01-p6-nf-lec05-kp01-p6-4.text: Both diagonals share the midpoint M

lec05kp01-u01-p6-nf-lec05-kp01-p6-22.name: fig:lec05-kp01-p6#22
lec05kp01-u01-p6-nf-lec05-kp01-p6-22.text: The B points add up to at most 0

lec05kp01-u01-p6-nf-lec05-kp01-p6-32.name: fig:lec05-kp01-p6#32
lec05kp01-u01-p6-nf-lec05-kp01-p6-32.text:
This is a proof for every line, not just for a few candidates.
Geometrically g(M) is both the average of the A end scores and of
the B end scores, so it cannot be positive and at most 0 at once.

lec05kp01-u01-p7-title.name: u01-p7-title
lec05kp01-u01-p7-title.text: However it is trained, one line cannot classify XOR perfectly: the lowest error is 1, not 0

lec05kp01-u01-p7-bridge.name: u01-p7-bridge
lec05kp01-u01-p7-bridge.text: The same expression must be above 0 for A and at most 0 for B, so no coefficients work. If every line fails, does more training help?

lec05kp01-u01-p7-nf-lec05-kp01-p7-1.name: fig:lec05-kp01-p7|Schematic error curve falling from 3 to 1 but never reaching the dashed 0 line; grid search over coefficients still leaves at least 1 XOR error.

lec05kp01-u01-p7-nf-lec05-kp01-p7-4.name: fig:lec05-kp01-p7#4
lec05kp01-u01-p7-nf-lec05-kp01-p7-4.text: Errors fall with training but never reach 0 (schematic)

lec05kp01-u01-p7-nf-lec05-kp01-p7-33.name: fig:lec05-kp01-p7#33
lec05kp01-u01-p7-nf-lec05-kp01-p7-33.text: A schematic, not a real experiment.

lec05kp01-u01-p7-nf-lec05-kp01-p7-34.name: fig:lec05-kp01-p7#34
lec05kp01-u01-p7-nf-lec05-kp01-p7-34.text:
Searching a grid of coefficients (−4 to 4, step 0.5),
XOR still has at least 1 error. (computed)

lec05kp01-u01-p7-nf-lec05-kp01-p7-36.name: fig:lec05-kp01-p7#36
lec05kp01-u01-p7-nf-lec05-kp01-p7-36.text: Capacity and training are two different questions

lec05kp01-u01-p7-nf-lec05-kp01-p7-37.name: term:Representational capacity
lec05kp01-u01-p7-nf-lec05-kp01-p7-37.text:
Representational capacity: whether the shape of the
model's boundary can express the answer at all.

lec05kp01-u01-p7-nf-lec05-kp01-p7-39.name: fig:lec05-kp01-p7#39
lec05kp01-u01-p7-nf-lec05-kp01-p7-39.text:
Common myth: more rounds, a smaller learning
rate or a fresh start should get all points right.

lec05kp01-u01-p7-nf-lec05-kp01-p7-40.name: fig:lec05-kp01-p7#40
lec05kp01-u01-p7-nf-lec05-kp01-p7-40.text:
These only look for fewer errors among the same family
of lines, and that family has no perfect answer.

lec05kp01-u01-p7-nf-lec05-kp01-p7-42.name: fig:lec05-kp01-p7#42
lec05kp01-u01-p7-nf-lec05-kp01-p7-42.text:
Whether training finds the best line and
whether the best line is good enough are
different questions. The lowest error is 1
point, not 0.

lec05kp01-u01-p8-title.text: Combine boundaries: two parallel lines make the strip 0.5 < s ≤ 1.5 holding exactly the A points

lec05kp01-u01-p8-bridge.name: u01-p8-bridge
lec05kp01-u01-p8-bridge.text: More training cannot help: the lowest error is 1, not 0. What must change for XOR to be separated?

lec05kp01-u01-p8-nf-lec05-kp01-p8-42.text: The s values are only 0, 1, 2, and A is exactly s = 1.

lec05kp01-u01-p8-nf-lec05-kp01-p8-45.text: Selected by the intersection of two judgments (supplementary).

lec05kp01-u01-p9-nf-lec05-kp01-p9-4.text: Implementation: points on the boundary, > and ≥ differ

steps.label: Three labelings
steps.speakerNotes: This is the first page of KP01. Three prerequisites: linear classifiers, scores and truth tables. The four inputs are (0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1), each coordinate 0 or 1. A label is the class a point must go to: A is a circle with output 1 and B is a square with output 0. OR outputs 1 if any input is 1, giving 0111 in order; AND outputs 1 only if both inputs are 1, giving 0001; exclusive OR, XOR, outputs 1 only if the inputs differ, giving 0110. The three panels have identical coordinates and differ only in labels. The A points of OR take three corners and those of AND only the top right, so one line looks enough for both; XOR puts same-class points on the diagonals, which is unclear (computed by program). Next, the next page covers scores and the rule.

steps.label: Score and rule
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the three labelings. This page states the rule. The score is g equal to w1 x1 plus w2 x2 plus w0 and the prediction is A if the score is above 0 and B otherwise, exactly 0 also B, and the rule may not change after seeing the labels; g equal to 0 is the line in the plot. Linearly separable means that some set of coefficients classifies every point correctly by this rule; the point is existence, not just the set found so far. Example: OR with w1 and w2 equal to 1 and w0 equal to minus 0.5 gives scores minus 0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 1.5; the last three are positive and called A, exactly OR (computed by program). Next, the next page covers the same line on XOR.

steps.label: Same line, XOR
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on scores and the rule. This page applies the same line g equal to x1 plus x2 minus 0.5 to XOR and substitutes point by point: (0,0) scores minus 0.5, predicted B, truth B; (0,1) scores 0.5, predicted A, truth A; (1,0) scores 0.5, predicted A, truth A; (1,1) scores 1.5, predicted A, truth B, wrong. The predictions equal OR and XOR has 1 error, accuracy 3 over 4 equal to 0.75, that is 75%, and with the 25% errors it adds up to 100% (computed by program). This is only the result for this one line and does not yet show that every line fails. Next, the next page covers three other lines.

steps.label: Three more lines
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the same line on XOR. This page tries three other lines. The first, g equal to x1 minus 0.5, predicts 0, 0, 1, 1 in order and has 2 errors. The second, g equal to x1 plus x2 minus 1.5, predicts 0, 0, 0, 1, cutting off only the top right corner; the errors are the two A points and one B point, 3 in all. The third, g equal to x1 minus x2, predicts 0, 0, 1, 0; the two points on the line score 0 and are called B by the rule, giving 1 error. All three have errors, but this is not a proof: too many lines are left untried (computed by program). Next, the next page covers the A diagonal.

steps.label: A diagonal
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on three other lines. This page supposes that some w1, w2, w0 classify XOR perfectly and lists the conditions they must meet. For the two A points: g(0,1) equals w2 plus w0 and must be above 0, and g(1,0) equals w1 plus w0 and must be above 0. A positive plus a positive stays positive, so adding gives w1 plus w2 plus 2 w0 above 0. Geometrically the two A points form a diagonal whose midpoint M is (1/2, 1/2); g is linear, so g(M) equals w1 plus w2 plus 2 w0 over 2, exactly the average of the two scores, and it is positive too (computed by program). Next, the next page covers the contradiction from B.

steps.label: B contradiction
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the A diagonal. This page looks at the two B points, whose scores must be at most 0 by the fixed rule: g(0,0) equals w0 at most 0 and g(1,1) equals w1 plus w2 plus w0 at most 0. Numbers at most 0 cannot add up to a positive: w0 plus w1 plus w2 plus w0 equals w1 plus w2 plus 2 w0, at most 0. This is exactly the same expression as for A: A requires it above 0 and B requires it at most 0, a contradiction. So no coefficients classify everything correctly, a proof for every line. Geometrically both diagonals share the midpoint M, and g(M) cannot be positive for one and at most 0 for the other. Next, the next page covers why training cannot help.

steps.label: Training cannot help
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the contradiction from B. This page addresses a common myth: more rounds, a smaller learning rate or a fresh initialization should get everything right. These only search for fewer errors among the same family of lines, perhaps reducing 3 errors to 1, but that family has no perfect answer and the lowest error is 1, not 0. The left chart is a schematic, not a real experiment; separately I searched a grid of coefficients (minus 4 to 4, step 0.5) and XOR still has at least 1 error (computed by program). Representational capacity is whether the shape of the model's boundary can express the answer at all; whether training finds the best line and whether the best line is good enough are two different questions. Next, the next page covers the strip between two lines.

steps.label: Strip
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on why training cannot help. This page shows that what must change is the combination of boundaries. What was ruled out is one linear score with a fixed threshold, not combinations of several boundaries. Let s equal x1 plus x2; the s values of the four XOR points are 0, 1, 1, 2 and A is exactly s equal to 1, so select it with the intersection of two judgments: the prediction is 1 if and only if 0.5 is below s and s is at most 1.5 (supplementary, computed by program). This verifies only the four Boolean points and does not fix a unique extension of XOR to the continuous plane. What changes is the set of boundary combinations the model allows, not a new set of old coefficients. The next KP asks how neurons build the two judgments. Next, the next page covers points on the boundary.

steps.label: Extension: Code
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the strip between two lines. This is an implementation reminder. After computing the scores point by point, produce predictions with score above 0 and compare them with the truth. Tests must include points on the boundary so that code using greater-or-equal does not disagree with text using greater-than. Take g equal to x1 minus x2: the scores at (0,0) and (1,1) are exactly 0; with greater-than the predictions are 0, 0, 1, 0 with 1 error; with greater-or-equal they are 1, 0, 1, 1 with 3 errors (computed by program). Half-integers are exact here; with general real data watch for floating-point error. Next, the next page covers exercise 1.

steps.label: Extension: Task 1
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on points on the boundary. This is the first exercise: compute the four inputs with g equal to x1 plus x2 minus 1.5 and check against AND and XOR. Solution: the formula is as above and g above 0 means A; substituting the four points gives scores minus 1.5, minus 0.5, minus 0.5, 0.5; only (1,1) is positive, so the predictions are B, B, B, A. Check: the AND truth is B, B, B, A, all right; for XOR, (0,1) and (1,0) are called B and (1,1) is called A, 3 wrong (computed by program). Next, the next page covers exercises 2 and 3.

steps.label: Extension: Task 2-3
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on exercise 1. These are exercises 2 and 3. Q2: does XOR fail because of few samples, noise, the learning rate or a limited boundary shape? Excluding one by one: the four inputs are all the data; the labels come straight from XOR and none is wrong; the contradiction holds for any coefficients, so the learning rate is irrelevant; only the limited boundary shape of a single line remains. Q3: which of OR, XOR, XNOR can one line separate? OR can, with g equal to x1 plus x2 minus 0.5 predicting B, A, A, A like OR; XNOR cannot, since same-class points still sit on the diagonals with only the labels swapped, so the same contradiction remains; the conclusion is that only OR is separable by one line (verified by exhaustive search). That ends this unit; next, move on to the next unit.
